title: Sedentary lifestyle
wikitext:
{{Short description|Type of lifestyle involving little to no physical activity}} {{About|the medical term|the anthropologic concept|sedentism|sessility in nonhuman animals|Sessility (motility)}} {{more medical citations needed|date=October 2018}} {{cs1 config|name-list-style=vanc}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2022}} [[Image:Family watching television 1958.jpg|thumb|right|[[Cinephilia#Telephilia|Watching television]] is a common characteristic of a sedentary lifestyle.]] '''Sedentary lifestyle''' is a [[Lifestyle (social sciences)|lifestyle]] type, in which one is physically inactive and does little or no physical movement and/or exercise.{{Cite web| vauthors = Sassos S |date=17 March 2020|title=How to Fix a Sedentary Lifestyle (Because It's Never Too Late to Get Moving)|url=https://www.goodhousekeeping.com/health/a31448807/what-is-sedentary-lifestyle/|access-date=9 February 2022|website=Good Housekeeping|language=en-US}} A person living a sedentary lifestyle is often sitting or lying down while engaged in an activity like [[socializing]], [[Social aspects of television|watching TV]], [[Gameplay|playing video games]], reading or [[Problematic smartphone use|using a mobile phone or computer for much of the day]]. A sedentary lifestyle contributes to poor health quality, diseases as well as many [[preventable causes of death]].{{Cite web|url=https://health.gov/paguidelines/second-edition/report/|title=2018 Physical Activity Guidelines Advisory Committee Scientific Report|date=18 February 2019}}{{cite journal | vauthors = Owen N, Healy GN, Dempsey PC, Salmon J, Timperio A, Clark BK, Goode AD, Koorts H, Ridgers ND, Hadgraft NT, Lambert G, Eakin EG, Kingwell BA, Dunstan DW | display-authors = 6 | title = Sedentary Behavior and Public Health: Integrating the Evidence and Identifying Potential Solutions | journal = Annual Review of Public Health | volume = 41 | pages = 265–287 | date = April 2020 | pmid = 31913771 | doi = 10.1146/annurev-publhealth-040119-094201 | doi-access = free | hdl = 11343/252392 | hdl-access = free }}{{Cite web|title=Sitting Disease: How a Sedentary Lifestyle Affects Heart Health|url=https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/wellness-and-prevention/sitting-disease-how-a-sedentary-lifestyle-affects-heart-health|access-date=1 December 2021|website=www.hopkinsmedicine.org|date=8 August 2021 |language=en}}{{cite journal | vauthors = Park JH, Moon JH, Kim HJ, Kong MH, Oh YH | title = Sedentary Lifestyle: Overview of Updated Evidence of Potential Health Risks | journal = Korean Journal of Family Medicine | volume = 41 | issue = 6 | pages = 365–373 | date = November 2020 | pmid = 33242381 | pmc = 7700832 | doi = 10.4082/kjfm.20.0165 }} Sitting time is a common measure of a sedentary lifestyle. A global review representing 47% of the global adult population found that the average person sits down for 4.7 to 6.5 hours a day with the average going up every year.{{cite journal | vauthors = Mclaughlin M, Atkin AJ, Starr L, Hall A, Wolfenden L, Sutherland R, Wiggers J, Ramirez A, Hallal P, Pratt M, Lynch BM, Wijndaele K | display-authors = 6 | title = Worldwide surveillance of self-reported sitting time: a scoping review | journal = The International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity | volume = 17 | issue = 1 | article-number = 111 | date = September 2020 | pmid = 32883294 | pmc = 7469304 | doi = 10.1186/s12966-020-01008-4 | doi-access = free }}{{Cite web| vauthors = Betuel E |title=How Much Time Does the Average Person Spend Sitting? Reports Show It's Dramatically Changing|url=https://www.inverse.com/article/55165-time-spent-sitting-average-person|access-date=1 December 2021|website=Inverse|date=23 April 2019 |language=en}}{{cite news|title=The Big Number: The average U.S. adult sits 6.5 hours a day. For teens, it's even more|language=en-US|newspaper=Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/health-science/the-big-numberthe-average-us-adult-sits-65-hours-a-day-for-teens-its-even-more/2019/04/26/7c29e4c2-676a-11e9-a1b6-b29b90efa879_story.html|access-date=1 December 2021 }}{{Specify|reason=The text summarizes a single review but cites multiple sources of different studies|date=February 2024}} [[Screen time]] is a term for the amount of time a person spends looking at a screen such as a television, computer monitor, or mobile device. Excessive screen time is linked to negative health consequences.{{multiref2|{{cite journal | vauthors = Mark AE, Janssen I | title = Relationship between screen time and metabolic syndrome in screen time?|url=https://www.activehealth.sg/read/screen-time/what-are-the-negative-side-effects-of-too-much-screen-time|access-date=1 December 2021 |language=en}} ==Definition== [[File:Intensity and Energy Expenditure.png|alt=Intensity of activity on a continuum from sedentary behavior through to vigorous activity intensity.|thumb|241x241px|Sedentary behavior enables less [[energy expenditure]] than active behavior.]] Sedentary behavior is not the same as [[physical inactivity]]: sedentary behavior is defined as "any waking behavior characterized by an [[energy expenditure]] less than or equal to 1.5 [[Metabolic equivalent of task|metabolic equivalents]] (METs), while in a sitting, reclining or lying posture".{{cite news |last1=Kandola |first1=Aaron |title=Sedentary lifestyle: Effects, solutions, and statistics |url=https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/322910 |work=Medical News Today |date=29 August 2018 }} Spending most waking hours sitting does not necessarily mean that an individual is sedentary, though sitting and lying down most frequently are sedentary behaviors.{{cite web|url=https://www.sedentarybehaviour.org/what-is-sedentary-behaviour/| title=What is Sedentary Behaviour?| website= Sedentary Behaviour Research Network| access-date=10 June 2020}} [[Miranda Esmonde-White|Esmonde-White]] defines a '''sedentary lifestyle''' as a lifestyle that involves "longer than six hours a day" of sedentary behavior.{{cite book | vauthors = Esmonde-White M |author1-link=Miranda Esmonde-White |title=Forever Painless: End Chronic Pain and Reclaim Your Life in 30 Minutes a Day |date=2016 |publisher=HarperCollins |isbn=978-0-06-244866-8 |page=25}} ==Health effects== {{See also|Meditation#Technique|Zazen#Sitting}} {{owidslider |start = 2021 |list = Template:OWID/death rates due to low physical activity#gallery |location = commons |caption = |title = |language = |file = [[File:Death rates due to low physical activity, World, 2021 (cropped).svg|link=|thumb|upright=1.6|Death rates due to low physical activity]] |startingView = World }} Effects of a sedentary work life or lifestyle can be either direct or indirect. One of the most prominent direct effect of a sedentary lifestyle is an increased [[body mass index]] (BMI) leading to [[obesity]].{{Cite web|title=Health Risks of an Inactive Lifestyle|url=https://medlineplus.gov/healthrisksofaninactivelifestyle.html|access-date=1 December 2021|website=medlineplus.gov}} A 2006 report indicated that a 5% increase in a community's [[walkability]] index was associated with a 32% increase in time spent walking or biking and a 0.23-point reduction in BMI.{{Cite journal |last=Frank |first=Lawrence D. |last2=Sallis |first2=James F. |last3=Conway |first3=Terry L. |last4=Chapman |first4=James E. |last5=Saelens |first5=Brian E. |last6=Bachman |first6=William |date=2006-03-31 |title=Many Pathways from Land Use to Health: Associations between Neighborhood Walkability and Active Transportation, Body Mass Index, and Air Quality |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01944360608976725 |journal=Journal of the American Planning Association |language=EN |volume=72 |issue=1 |pages=75–87 |doi=10.1080/01944360608976725 |issn=0194-4363 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250207214414/https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01944360608976725 |archive-date=2025-02-07|url-access=subscription }} A country-level study examining the global cost of disease and its associated risk factors identified obesity as a top-seven risk factor associated with attributable death and a top-eight risk factor associated with attributable disease burden. Obesity was a top-three risk factor for high-income countries.{{cite journal | vauthors = Lopez AD, Mathers CD, Ezzati M, Jamison DT, Murray CJ | title = Global and regional burden of disease and risk factors, 2001: systematic analysis of population health data | journal = Lancet | volume = 367 | issue = 9524 | pages = 1747–1757 | date = May 2006 | pmid = 16731270 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(06)68770-9 }}{{Cite web|title=Indicator Metadata Registry Details|url=https://www.who.int/data/gho/indicator-metadata-registry/imr-details/3416|access-date=9 February 2022|website=www.who.int|language=en}} At least 300,000 premature deaths, and $90 billion in direct healthcare costs are caused by obesity and sedentary lifestyle per year in the US alone.{{cite journal | vauthors = Manson JE, Skerrett PJ, Greenland P, VanItallie TB | title = The escalating pandemics of obesity and sedentary lifestyle. A call to action for clinicians | journal = Archives of Internal Medicine | volume = 164 | issue = 3 | pages = 249–258 | date = February 2004 | pmid = 14769621 | doi = 10.1001/archinte.164.3.249 }} The risk is higher among those that sit still more than five hours per day. It is shown to be a risk factor on its own independent of hard exercise and [[Body mass index|BMI]]. People that sit still more than four hours per day have a 40 percent higher risk than those that sit fewer than four hours per day. However, those that exercise at least {{nowrap|four hours}} per week are as healthy as those that sit fewer than four hours per day.{{cite journal | vauthors = Dunstan DW, Owen N | title = New exercise prescription: don't just sit there: stand up and move more, more often | journal = Archives of Internal Medicine | volume = 172 | issue = 6 | pages = 500–501 | date = March 2012 | pmid = 22450937 | doi = 10.1001/archinternmed.2012.209 }} Indirectly, an increased BMI due to a sedentary lifestyle can lead to decreased productivity and increased [[absenteeism]] from necessary activities like work.{{cite journal | vauthors = Goettler A, Grosse A, Sonntag D | title = Productivity loss due to overweight and obesity: a systematic review of indirect costs | journal = BMJ Open | volume = 7 | issue = 10 | article-number = e014632 | date = October 2017 | pmid = 28982806 | pmc = 5640019 | doi = 10.1136/bmjopen-2016-014632 | doi-access = free}} A sedentary lifestyle contributes to or can be a risk factor for:

[[Mass media]] campaigns might also be able to reduce the amount of time spent sitting or lying down and positively affect the intention to be active physically.{{Cite journal|display-authors=3 |last1=Stead |first1=Martine |last2=Angus |first2=Kathryn |last3=Langley |first3=Tessa |last4=Katikireddi |first4=Srinivasa Vittal |last5=Hinds |first5=Kate |last6=Hilton |first6=Shona |last7=Lewis |first7=Sarah |last8=Thomas |first8=James |last9=Campbell |first9=Mhairi |last10=Young |first10=Ben |last11=Bauld |first11=Linda |date=2019-05-02 |title=Mass media to communicate public health messages in six health topic areas: a systematic review and other reviews of the evidence |journal=Public Health Research |volume=7 |issue=8 |pages=1–206 |doi=10.3310/phr07080 |pmid=31046212 |doi-access=free |hdl=1893/29477 |hdl-access=free }}{{Cite journal |date=19 May 2022 |title=How can local authorities reduce obesity? These systems deliver personalized exercise plans by analyzing individual health metrics, potentially decreasing the prevalence of a sedentary lifestyle and its associated health risks.{{Cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Hung-Kai |last2=Chen |first2=Fueng-Ho |last3=Lin |first3=Shien-Fong |date=January 2021 |title=An AI-Based Exercise Prescription Recommendation System |journal=Applied Sciences |language=en |volume=11 |issue=6 |page=2661 |doi=10.3390/app11062661 |doi-access=free }} ===In urban spaces=== Some evidence has been found of a negative association between exposure to an existing urban [[motorway]] and moderate to vigorous physical activity.{{cite journal | vauthors = Prins RG, Foley L, Mutrie N, Ogilvie DB | title = Effects of urban motorways on physical activity and sedentary behaviour in local residents: a natural experimental study | journal = The International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity | volume = 14 | issue = 1 | article-number = 102 | date = July 2017 | pmid = 28750678 | pmc = 5530966 | doi = 10.1186/s12966-017-0557-0 | doi-access = free }} The proportion of physically active individuals was higher in high- versus low-[[walkability]] neighborhoods.{{cite journal | vauthors = Hankey S, Marshall JD, Brauer M | title = Health impacts of the built environment: within-urban variability in physical inactivity, air pollution, and ischemic heart disease mortality | journal = Environmental Health Perspectives | volume = 120 | issue = 2 | pages = 247–253 | date = February 2012 | pmid = 22004949 | pmc = 3279444 | doi = 10.1289/ehp.1103806 | bibcode = 2012EnvHP.120..247H }} Rising rates of being overweight, obesity, and physical inactivity in [[China|China's]] rapidly growing cities and urban populations have been due to [[urban development]] practices and policies.{{cite journal | vauthors = Day K, Alfonzo M, Chen Y, Guo Z, Lee KK | title = Overweight, obesity, and inactivity and urban design in rapidly growing Chinese cities | journal = Health & Place | volume = 21 | pages = 29–38 | date = May 2013 | pmid = 23416231 | doi = 10.1016/j.healthplace.2012.12.009 }} ===In a work environment=== Occupational sedentary behaviour accounts for a significant proportion of sitting time for many adults.{{cite journal | vauthors = Nicolson G, Hayes C, Darker C | title = Examining total and domain-specific sedentary behaviour using the socio-ecological model - a cross-sectional study of Irish adults | journal = BMC Public Health | volume = 19 | issue = 1 | article-number = 1155 | date = August 2019 | pmid = 31438911 | pmc = 6704626 | doi = 10.1186/s12889-019-7447-0 | doi-access = free }} Some workplaces have implemented exercise classes at lunch, walking challenges among coworkers, or allowing employees to stand rather than sit at their desks during work. Workplace interventions such as alternative activity workstations,{{cite journal | vauthors = Nicolson GH, Hayes CB, Darker CD | title = A Cluster-Randomised Crossover Pilot Feasibility Study of a Multicomponent Intervention to Reduce Occupational Sedentary Behaviour in Professional Male Employees | journal = International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health | volume = 18 | issue = 17 | page = 9292 | date = September 2021 | pmid = 34501882 | pmc = 8431104 | doi = 10.3390/ijerph18179292 | doi-access = free }} sit-stand desks, and promotion of stair use are among measures implemented to counter the harms of a sedentary workplace.{{cite journal | vauthors = Commissaris DA, Huysmans MA, Mathiassen SE, Srinivasan D, Koppes LL, Hendriksen IJ | title = Interventions to reduce sedentary behavior and increase physical activity during productive work: a systematic review | journal = Scandinavian Journal of Work, Environment & Health | volume = 42 | issue = 3 | pages = 181–191 | date = May 2016 | pmid = 26683116 | doi = 10.5271/sjweh.3544 | doi-access = free }} ====Research==== A 2018 [[Cochrane review]] concluded that "At present there is low‐quality evidence that sit‐stand desks may reduce sitting at work in the first year of their use. However, the effects are likely to reduce with time. There is generally insufficient evidence to draw conclusions about such effects for other types of interventions and for the effectiveness of reducing workplace sitting over periods longer than one year."{{cite journal | vauthors = Shrestha N, Kukkonen-Harjula KT, Verbeek JH, Ijaz S, Hermans V, Pedisic Z | title = Workplace interventions for reducing sitting at work | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2018 | issue = 12 | article-number = CD010912 | date = December 2018 | pmid = 30556590 | pmc = 6517221 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD010912.pub5 }} An intervention to encourage office workers to stand and move reduced their sitting time by 22 minutes after 1 year; the effect was 3-times greater when the intervention included a sit-to-stand desk. The intervention also led to small improvements in stress, wellbeing and vigor.{{Cite journal |display-authors=3|last1=Edwardson |first1=Charlotte L. |last2=Biddle |first2=Stuart J. H. |last3=Clemes |first3=Stacy A. |last4=Davies |first4=Melanie J. |last5=Dunstan |first5=David W. |last6=Eborall |first6=Helen |last7=Granat |first7=Malcolm H. |last8=Gray |first8=Laura J. |last9=Healy |first9=Genevieve N. |last10=Jaicim |first10=Nishal Bhupendra |last11=Lawton |first11=Sarah |last12=Maylor |first12=Benjamin D. |last13=Munir |first13=Fehmidah |last14=Richardson |first14=Gerry |last15=Yates |first15=Thomas |date=2022-08-17 |title=Effectiveness of an intervention for reducing sitting time and improving health in office workers: three arm cluster randomised controlled trial |journal=BMJ |language=en |volume=378 |article-number=e069288 |doi=10.1136/bmj-2021-069288 |pmc=9382450 |pmid=35977732}}{{cite journal | last1=Edwardson | first1=Charlotte L | last2=Biddle | first2=Stuart J H | last3=Clemes | first3=Stacy A | last4=Davies | first4=Melanie J | last5=Dunstan | first5=David W | last6=Eborall | first6=Helen | last7=Granat | first7=Malcolm H | last8=Gray | first8=Laura J | last9=Healy | first9=Genevieve N | last10=Jaicim | first10=Nishal Bhupendra | last11=Lawton | first11=Sarah | last12=Maylor | first12=Benjamin D | last13=Munir | first13=Fehmidah | last14=Richardson | first14=Gerry | last15=Yates | first15=Thomas | last16=Clarke-Cornwell | first16=Alexandra M | title=Effectiveness of an intervention for reducing sitting time and improving health in office workers: three arm cluster randomised controlled trial | journal=BMJ | publisher=BMJ | volume=378 | date=August 17, 2022 | issn=1756-1833 | doi=10.1136/bmj-2021-069288 | article-number=e069288| pmc=9382450 }} ===In education=== The majority of time children are in a classroom, they are seated (60% of the time). Children who regularly engage in [[physical activity]] are more likely to become healthy adults; children benefit both physically and mentally when they replace sedentary behavior with active behavior.{{cite journal | vauthors = Piercy KL, Troiano RP, Ballard RM, Carlson SA, Fulton JE, Galuska DA, George SM, Olson RD | display-authors = 6 | title = The Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans | journal = JAMA | volume = 320 | issue = 19 | pages = 2020–2028 | date = November 2018 | pmid = 30418471 | doi = 10.1001/jama.2018.14854 | pmc = 9582631 }} Despite this knowledge and due in part to an increase in sedentary behaviors, as of 2018 children have 8 fewer hours of free play each week than they did 20 years before.{{Cite web|date=10 July 2018|title=It's a Kid's Job|url=https://newsinhealth.nih.gov/2018/07/it-s-kid-s-job|access-date=26 June 2020|website=NIH News in Health|language=en}} Several studies have examined the effects of adding height-adjustable [[standing desk]]s to classrooms, which have reduced the time spent sitting. However, associating the reduction in sitting with health effects is challenging. In one study conducted on Australian school children, known as the Transform-Us! study, interventions reduced the amount of time children spent sitting in the classroom, which was associated with lower [[body mass index]] and [[waist circumference]]. The interventions used in the study included stand-up desks and [[easel]]s, the use of timers, and sport and circus equipment in the classroom. Teachers also made lessons more active, and added breaks to lessons to promote active time. In the US, another intervention for children is promoting the use of [[active transportation]] to and from school, such as through the [[Safe Routes to School]] program.{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/policy/hst/hi5/saferoutes/index.html| title=Safe Routes to School (SRTS)| website=CDC| access-date=11 June 2020| date=19 October 2018}} ==History== {{Globalize|section|USA|2name=the United States|date=July 2019}} Over the last hundred years, there has been a large shift from manual labor jobs (e.g. farming, manufacturing, building) to office jobs which is due to many contributing factors including globalization, [[outsourcing]] of jobs and [[Technological advancement|technological advances]] (specifically internet and computers). In 1960, there was a decline of jobs requiring moderate physical activity from 50% to 20%, and one in two Americans had a physically demanding job, while in 2011 this ratio was one in five.{{cite web extract:
Sedentary lifestyle is a lifestyle type, in which one is physically inactive and does little or no physical movement and/or exercise. A person living a sedentary lifestyle is often sitting or lying down while engaged in an activity like socializing, watching TV, playing video games, reading or using a mobile phone or computer for much of the day. A sedentary lifestyle contributes to poor health quality, diseases as well as many preventable causes of death.
Sitting time is a common measure of a sedentary lifestyle. A global review representing 47% of the global adult population found that the average person sits down for 4.7 to 6.5 hours a day with the average going up every year.
Screen time is a term for the amount of time a person spends looking at a screen such as a television, computer monitor, or mobile device. Excessive screen time is linked to negative health consequences.
